A: **Relay Bench and Break Station.** Option 1: Ticket queue where electrician fixes while visitors watch. Option 2: Two zones — four chairs at Repair Bench, eight at Break Station with dead appliances and tools. Arrivals without sign-up join Break Station first, diagnose junk with picture cards, then rotate to Bench as helpers. Chosen: Option 2 builds transferable skill. Example: Saturday visitor strips a dead kettle, tests fuse and continuity, then assists fixing another's toaster by checking its switch. Test: next week offer unfamiliar lamp fault; count Break-first visitors who attempt diagnosis versus Bench-only watchers.
B: **Alternating Beacon and Hearth.** Option 1: Both play best continuously and accept drift. Option 2: Clock-synced alternation — Beacon plays danceable set while Hearth plays quiet drone, swapping every 20 minutes past the hour. Chosen: Option 2 shepherds crowd without signaling. Example: At :00 A sparks singalong drawing drift; B keeps case visible with soft chords, collecting lingerers. At :20 they swap roles, crowd follows liveliness back. Noise cap never binds. Test: compare tip counts and headcounts at quiet end during its quiet slots versus a night both play full; alternation should raise quiet-end total.
C: **Numbered Drum with Ledger.** Option 1: Play drop-offs in arrival order. Option 2: Day volunteer sleeves each tape, issues numbered stub, logs duration and one-line description. Night plays blind draw without replacement across a multi-night cycle, filling three hours, logging numbers with start times. Ledger tracks plays per number; next night starts with least-played numbers, correcting imbalance. Chosen: Option 2. Example: Tape #47 plays 2:14 Tuesday; owner checks posted list Wednesday and hears description matches. Test: seed two identical-length marked tapes, compare play counts over a week versus arrival-order; drum-ledger should equalize counts and reveal misses.
D: **Four Crossings.** Option 1: One farewell festival with commemorative plaque. Option 2: Four seasonal meetings tied to crossing rituals — autumn story walks, winter light and sound recording, spring sorting of salvaged bolts, lamps, and deck planks, summer vote on reuse. Daily crossers tag valued spots with ribbons that become salvage priority. Chosen: Option 2 embeds use into fabric. Example: Commuters mark sunrise viewpoint; its rail section becomes overlook benches on new crossing with etched names. Test: survey new-bridge users to name one reused element's origin versus plaque-only bridge; reuse should score higher recognition.
